We consider a perfect monitoring instrument that records the instantaneous molecular density throughout a finite region without perturbing the concentration field or distinguishing molecular identities. The standard Berg-Purcell estimator weights all positions uniformly. Here we derive the optimal spatial weighting within a large class of unbiased estimators for both concentration and gradient sensing. Variance minimization maps to an electrostatic problem. Surprisingly, although the instrument monitors the entire volume, the optimal estimator assigns all weight to its boundary, reducing the uncertainty in both concentration and gradient sensing. We extend the results to arbitrary geometries and spatial dimensions.

items.title: Phase Transitions in Learning Driven by Extremal Data
items.summary: We study an extremal regression problem, an example of multiple instance learning (MIL), where the predictors are given as multisets, called bags. The bag elements (called instances) possess hidden labels which are pooled to produce an observed bag-level label. Max pooling is common in MIL applications, but gives rise to vanishing gradients. To handle this, modern MIL pipelines approximate the max with a softmax, treating the sharpness as a learnable parameter, denoted $λ$. When the max pooling model is the true data generating process, learning will be successful when $λ$ is increased during gradient descent, thereby driving the dynamics into regions of parameter space with vanishing gradients. To understand the conditions under which gradient descent breaks down, we study a minimal model and derive a low dimensional projection of the gradient flow in the joint limit of large bags $n$ and high dimension $d$ with $α=\ln n/d$ fixed. The flow has two distinct phase transitions: an intrinsic freezing transition related to the random energy model of disordered systems, and a retrieval transition occurring in modern Hopfield networks. Numerical simulation confirms both the phase diagram and the convergence of the finite-size training gradient to its predicted asymptotic form.

items.title: Impact of Torque Ripple Induced Angular Oscillations on Maxwell Pressure Harmonics in Permanent-Magnet Synchronous Machines
items.summary: Torque ripple in electrical machines is a wellknown source of noise and vibration. While numerous studies focus on control strategies to mitigate this ripple, the feedback mechanism by which the resulting mechanical oscillations influence the electromagnetic forces remains less explored. This paper presents a detailed investigation into the impact of torque ripple on the rotor angular dynamics and the subsequent generation of new harmonics in the Maxwell pressure distribution. We first develop an analytical model for a rigid rotor subjected to a single torque harmonic, revealing the inherently non-linear nature of the angular response. This analysis demonstrates the creation of new harmonics in the rotor motion and a slight reduction in the mean rotational speed. The study is then extended to a flexible rotor model incorporating torsional modes, solved using the Finite Element Method. Finally, we introduce a strongly coupled magneto-mechanical model, based on the subdomain method, to quantify how these rotor oscillations modulate the air-gap magnetic field. The results show a new modulated spatio-temporal harmonic distribution in the Maxwell pressure spectrum, which is not predicted by conventional uncoupled models. These findings are crucial for high-fidelity Noise, Vibration, and Harshness (NVH) analysis, as these additional pressure waves can excite stator structural modes.

items.title: Distinct weak antisymmetric interactions shape human brain functions as probability fluxes
items.summary: The functional computation of the human brain is hypothesized to arise from the collective behaviour of the underlying neural network. A method based on an idea from equilibrium statistical mechanics has been applied to infer the underlying interaction network among the brain regions from whole-brain imaging, but recent studies have challenged the equilibrium assumption. Without equilibrium, how does the human brain encode its function in biased state transitions? Here we show that the probability fluxes, which quantify the irreversibility of state transitions, exhibit unique, task-dependent patterns in spontaneous and task-induced whole-cerebral-cortex activity. We then fit an Ising model with asymmetric interactions and reveal that the symmetric interactions among the brain regions are strong and task-independent, whereas the antisymmetric interactions are weak and task-dependent, and that the fitted model reproduces the observed fluxes for most tasks. Our results indicate that the human brain performs its functional computation by subtly modifying the antisymmetric part of the interactions among the brain regions, offering a new explanation for how a similar interaction network supports diverse brain functions. The method can be applied to the time-series data of other high-dimensional many-body systems to reveal the probability fluxes and infer the underlying interactions among components.

items.title: Fault-tolerant hyper-Ramsey spectroscopy of optical clock transitions with dynamical decoupling
items.summary: A probe laser field that interrogates an atomic transition also shifts it. Although Hyper-Ramsey (HR) spectroscopy was developed to mitigate these light-induced frequency shifts, the technique remains sensitive to probe intensity fluctuations. In this work, we introduce a novel class of dynamically decoupled hyper-Ramsey (DDHR) sequences that utilize a modified refocusing pulse to effectively eliminate this residual sensitivity. This three-pulse interferometric protocol significantly enhances the contrast of quantum interference fringes while providing robust immunity against probe-induced frequency shifts, even in the presence of external field inhomogeneities. We experimentally validate both HR and DDHR protocols on the NQCH and \textcolor{blue}{IQM} superconducting quantum processor, demonstrating an error scaling that is rigorously consistent with theoretical simulations of the optical clock regime. DDHR spectroscopy yields superior suppression of residual probe-induced frequency shifts compared to the standard HR scheme under probe amplitude fluctuation and decoherence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the implementation of composite refocusing pulses, derived from a Pascal binomial tree architecture, gives substantial resilience against technical pulse area imperfections. Ultimately, fault-tolerant, dynamically decoupled hyper-clocks will offer a promising experimental platform for the evaluation of advanced, NMR-inspired DDHR sequences of multiple refocusing pulses holding significant potential for high-precision matter/antimatter quantum sensing and rigorous tests of fundamental physics within harsh electromagnetic environments.

items.title: Extending AMIRAL's blind deconvolution of Adaptive Optics corrected images with Markov chain Monte Carlo methods
items.summary: Adaptive optics (AO) corrected image restoration is particularly difficult, as it suffers from the lack of knowledge on the point spread function (PSF) in addition to usual difficulties. An efficient approach is to marginalize the object out of the problem and to estimate the PSF and (object and noise) hyperparameters only, before deconvolving the object using these estimates. Recent works have applied this marginal blind deconvolution method, combined to a parametric model of the PSF, to a series of AO corrected astronomical and satellite images. In this communication, we propose a new restoration method, which consists in choosing the Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) estimator and computing the latter thanks to a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. We validate our method by means of realistic simulations, in two very different contexts: an astronomical observation on VLT/SPHERE and a ground-based LEO satellite observation on a 1.52m telescope. Finally, we present results on experimental images for both applications.

items.title: Forecasting carbon-risk hotspots ahead of the extreme 2026 El Niño
items.summary: A potentially super El Niño is forecasted in 2026, raising the need to anticipate land carbon-cycle risks before its impacts unfold. We develop a prospective early-warning framework that uses dynamic global vegetation models driven by an ensemble of ECMWF seasonal climate forecasts and machine-learning burned area predictions. Forecasts indicate a $0.23 \pm 0.21$ PgC reduction in global net biome productivity in the second half of 2026, with hotspots of sink weakening in eastern South America and elevated fire risk in Southeast Asia.

items.title: Atomic thermometry in optical lattice clocks: model discrepancies and their impact on lattice light shifts
items.summary: Accurate measurement of atomic temperature is fundamental for a wide range of applications, from quantum sensing to precision metrology. In optical lattice clocks, precise characterization of atomic temperature is required to minimize systematic uncertainties at the $10^{-18}$ level. In this work, we investigate atomic temperature measurements in the ytterbium optical clock developed at INRIM, IT-Yb1, employing sideband and transverse Doppler spectroscopy across a wide range of trapping conditions in a one-dimensional optical lattice. By implementing clock-line-mediated Sisyphus cooling [Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 053401 (2024)], we reduce the atomic temperature and enable operation at shallower lattice depths down to $D = 50\,E_\text{R}$, where $E_\text{R}$ is the photon recoil energy. We compare temperature estimates obtained from the perturbed harmonic oscillator model with those derived using a Born-Oppenheimer model [Phys. Rev. A 101, 053416 (2020)]. Discrepancies of up to a factor of four are observed between the temperature estimates obtained with the two approximations. We assess the impact of these modeling differences on the evaluation of lattice light shifts and find relative frequency deviations of up to $8\times10^{-17}$. Although sufficiently low atomic temperatures and the consistent use of theoretical models reduce these discrepancies to the low $10^{-18}$ level, these results motivate further investigations that will be relevant to state-of-the-art optical lattice clocks.

items.title: Low optical loss electrical isolation for multi-section monolithic GaSb-based photonic circuits
items.summary: Monolithic photonic integrated circuits (PICs) platforms exploiting III-V materials combine passive and active waveguide structures in multi-section optoelectronic device architectures. Their operation requires high electrical isolation between adjacent functional sections without compromising the optical signal. This fundamental requirement is addressed for GaSb-based waveguides, which are known to exhibit high conductivity of p-type layers reducing the electrical isolation capability. To this end, a co-designed electrical-optical isolation strategy based on using deeply etched strip waveguides combined with adiabatic ridge-to-strip waveguide tapers in GaSb-based multiple-quantum-well heterostructures is proposed. While deep etching alone enables isolation resistances of up to 40 k-ohm, it severely degrades optical propagation. By introducing optimized adiabatic tapers, we demonstrate good optical performance as single-mode continuous-wave lasing in a two-section device with integrated absorber, while maintaining an isolation resistance of 17.3 k-ohm; this corresponds to an approximately 17-fold improvement over previously reported GaSb two-section devices. The approach establishes a critical building block for the development of monolithic GaSb-based PICs operating above 2 um.

items.title: Spin-Adapted Spin-Flip Tamm-Dancoff Approximation (XSF-TDA) for Singlet-Triplet Gaps in MR-TADF and INVEST Emitters
items.summary: In this work, we assess the recently introduced spin-adapted TDA for spin-flip-down excitations (XSF-TDA) [Mol. Phys. e2631735 (2026)] as a practical approach to this problem. Starting from a high-spin restricted open-shell Kohn--Sham reference, XSF-TDA generates spin-adapted low-spin roots arising from open--open (OO), core--open (CO), open--virtual (OV), and core--virtual (CV) types of spin-flip-down excitations. Across four application sets comprising 243 benchmark cases, XSF-TDA substantially reduces the systematic positive bias observed for TDA and unrestricted spin-flip TDA (USF-TDA). With the B3LYP functional, XSF-TDA reduces the equal-set-weighted macro-MAE relative to USF-TDA from 0.252 eV (0.158 eV) to 0.102~eV (0.056~eV) with the ALDA0 (multicollinear) kernel. Its accuracy is competitive with state-specific $Δ$DFT and quasiparticle-energy DFT (QE-DFT), while being able to provide deeper mechanistic insight through the response vector. In particular, spin-adapted CV configurations provide selected higher-excitation character that strengthens the OO--CV dynamical-spin-polarization channel, which preferentially stabilizes the singlet states. We also identify an INVEST emitter with appreciable OO--OV mixing, suggesting a possible additional contribution to singlet stabilization when the CV contribution is small. The XSF-TDA method therefore provides practical singlet--triplet gap predictions together with interpretable state analysis for the screening and mechanistic understanding of MR-TADF and INVEST emitters.

items.title: Higher-order corrections to the field shift in atomic systems
items.summary: Differences in nuclear charge distributions between isotopes lead to small changes in atomic spectra known as the field shift. While largely proportional to the change in the mean-square nuclear radius, the field shift also contains higher-order contributions with different dependencies on nuclear moments. Their knowledge is required in searches for new physics using King plots, since they contribute to deviations from King-plot linearity observed experimentally in recent studies. We present a systematic expansion of the field-shift energies in terms of nuclear parameters and test its validity against direct numerical calculations for H-like ions. We also compute leading- and higher-order field-shift corrections for alkali-like systems from Li-like to Rb-like ions, and find that their ratios are nearly independent of the ionic charge state, agreeing with the corresponding hydrogenic $1s$ ratios on a sub-percent level. Motivated by these findings, we introduce an approximation in which these ratios are assumed to be independent of the electronic configuration. It is shown that, within this approximation, higher-order field-shift corrections do not induce King-plot nonlinearities. We conclude that only the small contributions beyond this approximation can contribute to the nonlinearities observed experimentally.

items.title: Adaptive Entangled Neurons in the Brain and Natural Intelligence Simulations for Artificial General Intelligence
items.summary: Understanding the brain's mechanisms is crucial in neuroscience, particularly for simulating natural intelligence and advancing artificial general intelligence (AGI). Liu et al. (2024) and Deco et al. (2025) propose that quantum entanglement may underlie the synchronization of millions of neurons, introducing the Liu-Chen-Ao (LCA) hypothesis of entangled nerve fibers. However, directly testing this idea remains challenging. Here we employ a nonlocal many-body wave equation, introducing a generalized probability-wave framework to model collective behaviors among adaptive, interacting agents, particles, or neurons. This approach enables testable eigenmodes, offering an indirect means of examining the LCA hypothesis by observing patterns in collective trading behaviors. These patterns, rooted in behavioral psychology, are thought to mirror the internal brain's decision-making and underlying mechanisms. Our analysis of Chinese intraday stock market data shows that adaptive entangled game modes explain 82%-94% of decision patterns, sharply contrasting neoclassical finance predictions assuming independent rational agents. Additionally, 2-12% of actions adapt to news, events, and environmental changes, marked by rapid equilibrium shifts, while truly independent behaviors make up less than 5%. These results empirically support the LCA hypothesis and underscore the need to simulate the brain's mechanisms and generate adaptive, entangled modules for AGI. They also expose the shortcomings of conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs) that depend on vast, opaque parameters. By combining ANN-based AI with probability-wave-based entangled brain simulations, machine learning enables the creation of human-like processing units (HPUs). Such HPUs promise more efficient and robust AGI, particularly for embodied intelligence and robotics.

items.title: Frequency Attraction and Repulsion in Lasers with Complex Mutual Coupling
items.summary: We experimentally investigate laser synchronization under complex mutual coupling, featuring both dissipative and dispersive components. Using a reconfigurable digital degenerate cavity laser with precise control over system parameters, we show that complex coupling can induce both frequency attraction and repulsion, in contrast to common models of coupled oscillators. Furthermore, we show that these frequency shifts can be exploited to significantly enhance global synchronization in multi-laser arrays. Comparison with numerical and theoretical results indicate that amplitude dynamics of complex coupled lasers play an important role in the observed phenomena. Our results establish a versatile platform for exploring non-Hermitian physics and topological states in tailored laser networks.

items.title: How Far Can Foundation Models Be Distilled for Efficient Jet Tagging?
items.summary: Jet tagging is one of the most important applications of machine learning at the Large Hadron Collider. Recent models build in more physics knowledge or rely on large-scale pretraining, but the experiments place strict limits on their inference cost. Knowledge distillation can transfer their performance to small students that are cheap to run. We ask which properties of a teacher help the student, how small a student can get and how close it can come to the state of the art. On a jet tagging benchmark, we distil six teachers that differ in architecture, symmetry and pretraining, including two foundation models, into five small students. Every teacher improves every student, and the gain depends mainly on the strength of the teacher. We then shrink our two strongest distilled students, Transformer and L-GATr-slim, in width and in depth. With 20 thousand parameters, a distilled L-GATr-slim outperforms every published jet tagger trained from scratch at a fraction of the inference cost of every teacher. Even with two thousand parameters, it matches ParT, a model with a thousand times as many parameters. We also study what the students learn from their teachers. Our benchmark of inference cost shows that students of the same size can differ by almost an order of magnitude in speed. We release the code and the weights of all trained models.

items.title: Urban climate regressions require representative monitoring networks
items.summary: Land use regression models relate intra-urban air temperature to spatial predictors such as building volume, tree canopy cover and topography, and are increasingly used to produce fine-scale temperature maps. However, the accuracy of these estimates can be compromised by unrepresentative monitoring networks. Here we show that reference weather station networks, designed for regional rather than intra-urban monitoring, sample only a narrow portion of a city's spatial heterogeneity, missing both the densely built core and the cool, vegetated periphery that set the two ends of the urban temperature range. As a result, city-wide predictions underestimate temperature differences, in ways that cross-validation against the station measurements does not detect. Using Zurich, Switzerland, as a case study, we compare multiple linear regression, generalized additive models and random forests as up to 117 low-cost temperature sensors are added to the four reference weather stations. When trained on reference stations alone, all three models achieve comparable cross-validated performance. As low-cost sensors broaden the sampled spatial heterogeneity, multiple linear regression scores lower on both metrics, whereas the non-linear models remain at their reference-only level. Although a third of the low-cost sensors already recovers nearly the full predicted temperature range, which predictors are identified, and with which sign, is determined by the station sample rather than the model class. At full coverage, only multiple linear regression leaves significant residual spatial autocorrelation, suggesting a linear form unable to capture non-linear responses of air temperature to urban form. Drawing on landscape ecology research on focal site study design, we provide a transferable framework for diagnosing station network representativeness and improving the reliability of city-wide environmental maps.

items.title: Photon Correlations Control Quantum Fisher Information in Coherent Multidimensional Spectroscopy
items.summary: Coherent multidimensional spectroscopy probes interactions and dynamics of molecular systems through nonlinear optical signals. Quantum light excitation has been explored as a means of controlling these signals, raising the question of how excitation-light correlations affect the precision of molecular parameter estimation from the emitted signal. In this work, we show that photon-number correlations and two-photon coherence play distinct roles in encoding molecular information in the emitted rephasing signal. In the weak-emission regime and within the single Schmidt pair approximation, we derive a normally ordered information law in which the joint photon-number moment and the squared magnitude of the two-photon coherence weight the amplitude and phase sensitivities of the molecular response, respectively. For matched temporal modes and mean photon numbers in each input mode, two-mode squeezed vacuum enhances both weights relative to coherent excitation, whereas independent displaced squeezing preserves the amplitude weight but reduces the phase weight. The background population and its parameter dependence also affect the total quantum Fisher information, which therefore cannot be inferred from the coherent mean-field signal alone. We derive a leading-order bound on its enhancement over coherent excitation when the background population is nonnegative and common to the compared sources. These findings provide criteria for selecting excitation sources according to how the target molecular parameter affects the amplitude and phase of the response.

items.title: Quasi-Phase-Matched Second Harmonic Generation in Poling-Free Lithium Niobate Microrings with Surface Molecular Pattern
items.summary: Thin film lithium niobate (TFLN) is a promising integrated photonic platform owing to its large quadratic nonlinearity enabling vital applications such as second-harmonic generation (SHG), optical parametric amplification, and spontaneous parametric down-conversion. However, to achieve high SH conversion efficiency, quasi-phase matching (QPM) through periodic electrical poling is typically required, which remains challenging in certain applications like multiple-ring coupled devices. Here, we demonstrate a surface molecule patterning strategy to enable QPM in a poling-free TFLN microring for SHG. An on-chip normalized conversion efficiency of approximately 11.5%/W is obtained in the poling-free TFLN microring with surface molecular pattern, showing an approximate 400-fold improvement compared to the same microring without surface molecular pattern. This approach offers a versatile route to engineer interfacial nonlinear interactions for nonlinear optics and quantum photonics applications and may be extended to multiple-ring coupled resonators and other platforms.

items.title: Bias-Modulated Electronically-Tunable Optoelectronic Chromatic Dispersion in Ge PN Photodiodes
items.summary: Optoelectronic Chromatic Dispersion (OED) is a source of significant wavelength-dependent current in photodiodes, offering a pathway to computational spectroscopy in a photodiode-only platform without the need for additional optical or mechanical components. Previous studies have activated OED through light modulation. Here, we present a theoretical and experimental investigation of bias-modulated OED in the C- and L-bands in a Ge PN photodiode, where the applied bias voltage is modulated sinusoidally, and the optical illumination is held constant. The spectral response is due to wavelength-dependent optical absorption together with bias-dependent competition between carrier drift, displacement current, and mobile-charge screening. With the RF phase-shift technique, the maximum measured OED sensitivity is +4.13 deg/nm in the L-band, significantly larger than that of light-modulated OED in Ge. The 15 mdeg phase-noise floor yields a spectral resolution of 3.6 pm. These results establish bm-OED as an electronically reconfigurable dispersive mechanism for applications in chip-scale computational spectrometers, photonic integrated circuits (PICs), on-chip RF photonics, and wavelength-division multiplexing.

items.title: Tuning Thermal Memory and Dissipation in Colloidal Glasses via Microgel Particle Stiffness
items.summary: The Kovacs effect, characterized by nonlinear, path-dependent structural recovery, is a hallmark of glassy systems. In soft colloidal microgel glasses, the stiffness of the constituent particles governs their deformation, swelling, rearrangement, and response to external stimuli, thereby dictating the path-dependent structural recovery of these jammed non-equilibrium systems. To investigate this influence, microgels of different stiffnesses were synthesized by adjusting the concentration of the polar crosslinker, N, N'-methylenebisacrylamide (MBA). The relaxation of the storage and loss moduli was measured using oscillatory rheology under diverse temperature ramp rates, and cryo-FESEM imaging provided direct visualization of the underlying particle packing. While the rapid adaptability of soft particles and the kinetic arrest of stiff ones suppresses Kovacs asymmetry, intermediate-stiffness particles exhibit moderate thermoresponsivity, traversing distinct energy landscapes on heating and cooling to maximize asymmetry and dissipation. Cryo-FESEM micrographs, displaying gel-like networks in soft particle suspensions, dense packing in stiff particle suspensions, and disordered, compact structures in intermediate-stiffness systems, corroborate these findings. Our results demonstrate that intermediate-stiffness PNIPAM microgels optimize structural recovery, rendering them promising candidates for forming colloidal glasses and establishing Kovacs asymmetry as a robust probe of non-equilibrium dynamics in glassy systems.

items.title: Closing the Loop in Epitaxy with Machine Learning: Joint Optimization of Growth and Geometry in On-Chip Lasers
items.summary: Achieving device-to-device reproducibility is a critical bottleneck for scalable photonic integrated circuits, as subtle variations in bottom-up epitaxial growth and fabrication severely limit yield. We present a machine learning workflow for III-V multi-quantum well microring lasers that first optimizes growth and geometry parameters via multi-objective Bayesian optimization, then leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to attribute residual device-to-device variability to its underlying sources. By explicitly targeting threshold variance alongside absolute performance, we demonstrate 100% lasing yield across all designs. The optimized multi-quantum well microring laser fields achieved a median lasing threshold of $16~μ\mathrm{J}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{pulse}^{-1}$, a $73\%$ reduction in threshold variance relative to the previously reported best values, and a median emission wavelength of $1333~\mathrm{nm}$, in the telecommunications O-band. Furthermore, to diagnose residual performance dispersion under nominally identical conditions, VAEs were used to isolate the key components of device morphology that impact performance. This analysis successfully decoupled geometric from material disorder, quantitatively linking previously unmeasured morphological variations to population-level threshold fluctuations. This data-driven workflow bridges the gap between fundamental epitaxy and reliable manufacturing, establishing a generalizable blueprint for designing and yield-optimizing complex, non-linear optoelectronic devices.

items.title: Euclidean Fourier Neural Operators
items.summary: Fourier neural operators (FNOs) provide an efficient framework for learning mappings between function spaces as they are, by construction, independent of the grid resolution at which they are trained and evaluated. However, FNOs are not independent of the periodic domain they are applied to: their discrete spectral weights are indexed by integer Fourier mode numbers, which correspond to physical wavevectors. When applied to a different domain, the same trained weights act at different wavevectors, and the FNO silently represents a different operator. This makes FNOs unsuitable for tasks where transfer across domains is crucial. We propose Euclidean Fourier neural operators~(EFNOs) as a domain-independent alternative to FNOs. By parameterizing the spectral kernel as a continuous function of the physical wavevector, the EFNO can learn operators that act consistently across periodic domains of varying shape and size. We evaluate the EFNO on a simple heat equation and on a practically relevant materials science task of learning exchange-correlation potentials across different crystal structures, and demonstrate that the EFNO is able to generalize to unseen grid sizes and domains.

items.title: SoLiD26: A First Principles Solid-Liquid Interface Dataset for Machine-learned Interatomic Potentials
items.summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) enable simulations of larger atomistic systems over longer timescales than traditional ab initio methods but require large, diverse training data. Existing datasets lack comprehensive sampling of solid-liquid interfaces, which exhibit complex phenomena such as solvent layering and surface reconstruction critical for energy and catalytic materials. Here, we present SoLiD26, a curated solid-liquid interface dataset of 15.4 million first-principles structures with up to 576 atoms and 15 chemical elements for training and evaluating MLIPs. The structures were compiled from density functional theory (DFT) calculations, with most configurations originating from ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. SoLiD26 includes aqueous coinage metal interfaces, electrode-electrolyte systems, and selected bulk reference structures, calculated with VASP using the PBE functional and D3 dispersion corrections. The application of SoLiD26 for training and evaluating MLIPs is demonstrated with a suite of MACE models on a simple training, validation and test split. This dataset provides a valuable resource for advancing MLIP development targeted at modelling solid-liquid interfaces in electrochemical and catalytic systems.

items.title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion
items.summary: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.

items.title: Dual Transverse Vortex-Spin-Momentum Locking in Rotating-Wave Structured Light
items.summary: We theoretically investigate the transverse Poynting momentum and transverse spin angular momentum in circularly polarized rotating-wave structured light, and reveal a pair of dual transverse vortex-spin-momentum locking. The transverse Poynting momentum exhibits a $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetric locking structure, being controlled independently by either the polarization or vortex handedness, yet invariant under their simultaneous reversal. Meanwhile, the transverse spin angular momentum is independent of the polarization but endowed with a crucial vortex-dependence inheriting such vortex-dependence from the Poynting momentum via curl operation. This finding expands the understanding of transverse optical linear and angular momenta in structured light and opens a new paradigm for vortex-spin-controlled optical manipulation.

items.title: Light pulse propagation through a dielectric slab. I. Retarded integral equations and their local finite-difference solution
items.summary: We describe the propagation of a nonresonant light pulse normally incident on a thin dielectric slab using an integral-equation approach to electromagnetism. This emerges naturally from the microscopic picture of the material as made of polarizable atoms, confined within the material vacuum volume by their bonding interactions, each responding to the input radiation pulse as well as to the re-radiated pulses of the other atoms to which it is causally connected. The retarded integral equations are shown to be exactly equivalent to a local wave equation coupled to an auxiliary Lorentz-oscillator equation, which we solve numerically with a finite-difference time-domain scheme. For a slab thick enough that the front- and back-surface reflections are temporally separated, the front-surface reflectivity extracted from the simulation agrees with the Fresnel formula to within 1 percent, and the back-surface echo appears at exactly the expected round-trip delay. For a slab thinner than one optical cycle, the multiply-reflected wavelets overlap and interfere, and a full space-time map of the field directly visualizes the build-up of thin-film-like interference in the time domain. The material parameters used here are illustrative rather than fitted to measured data, and the numerical scheme is verified by an explicit grid-convergence study. In a companion paper (Paper II) the retarded integral equations are solved directly, without the local reformulation, and the two independent numerical solutions are shown to agree.

items.title: A Machine Learning Approach to Finslerian Cosmological Dark Energy Model
items.summary: Modified extensions of the standard cosmological models often introduce complex parameter degeneracies that severely impact sampling convergence of the parameter space while analyzing the model observationally. In this work, we present an accelerated Bayesian inference technique using a Heteroscedastic Deep Ensemble with Monte Carlo Dropout incorporating distance-gated local residual corrections to emulate complex likelihood surfaces and avoid extrapolation beyond the trained region. We demonstrate this methodology on a unified dark energy cosmological model equipped with Finsler geometry. The model is studied using the recent observational datasets, including Cosmic Chronometers (CC), Pantheon$+$SH$0$ES, and DESI DR$2$ BAO measurements. While the conventional sampling procedure struggles with slow mixing of parameter chains ($τ_{max}=1578.3$), the neural network, specially trained densely in high likelihood regions, yields converged and highly resolved posterior distributions of the model parameters without significantly compromising the minimum chi-square value. We further discuss the results for physical inferences and also compare the present dark energy model with $Λ\text{CDM}$ statistically using AIC and BIC.

items.title: Sweep-Direction-Dependent Level-Attraction- and Level-Repulsion-Like Signatures in a Twisted, Helically Corrugated Microwave Resonator
items.summary: We investigate photon--photon interactions in a mechanically tunable, helically corrugated rectangular microwave resonator. Mechanical twisting modifies the electromagnetic helicity and resonant frequencies of the supported modes, allowing pairs of electromagnetic modes to be tuned into near-degeneracy. Transmission magnitude and phase measurements reveal two distinct responses: a level-attraction-like response characterised by converging antiresonances and a sharp phase variation appearing as a $2π$ discontinuity in the wrapped transmission phase, and a level-repulsion-like response characterised by an anticrossing-like transmission feature. For the mode-interaction regions investigated, reversing the twist sweep direction interchanges these responses. We discuss mechanical hysteresis and changes in electromagnetic backscattering and modal interference as possible origins of this behaviour. These observations suggest a potential route towards microwave devices with mechanically switchable level-attraction-like and level-repulsion-like transmission responses.

items.title: Data-driven and physics-guided hindcasting of measured wave spectra
items.summary: Short-range hindcasts of measured wave spectra are evaluated using a recurrent model initialized by one hourly buoy spectrum and supplied with local wind, fetch and depth. Measurements from three Baltic Sea stations are combined for training in 2017--2020, validation in 2021 and testing in 2022. ERA5 reanalysis supplies winds throughout the twelve-hour prediction interval. The comparison examines supervision of spectral variance, peak frequency and peak amplitude, followed by empirical wind-sea bounds and a local relaxation constraint. Variance and peak-frequency supervision gives the lowest spectral error within the data-driven comparison, whereas additional peak-amplitude supervision gives the lowest wave-height error. In the matched physical comparison, relaxation reduces height RMSE by 5.01\% to \PhPtwoHs{}~cm. Extending this constraint through hours 13--24, without spectral targets at those hours, reduces primary spectral RMSE by 2.31\% to \PhPthreeSpec{}~$\unitE$. Upper-bound constraints increase errors. Wind-condition comparisons show spectral gains from extended relaxation in increasing, decreasing and steady strong winds, with little change in steady weak winds. The results support modest, objective-dependent benefits from local physical guidance. Wave-height scores concern the retained frequency band, and operational forecasting and transfer to independent stations remain to be evaluated.

items.title: Einstein's theory of Brownian motion: The non-Fickian normal diffusion
items.summary: Einstein's theory of diffusion defines what is considered {\it normal diffusion}. Historically, Einstein considered homogeneous diffusion characterised by a diffusion constant in his original calculations, resulting in what is known as {\it Fickian} diffusion, which thermally relaxes concentration inhomogeneities. However, in the same derivation of Einstein, the seed of generalisation of the theory to {\it non-Fickian} diffusion in the presence of space-dependent diffusivity is hidden. This indicates that non-Fickian diffusion, which can drive concentration inhomogeneities, can also be normal diffusion. The present article discusses the origin of the {\it normal} non-Fickian diffusion in Einstein's theory of diffusion.

items.title: Binder migration across film consolidation and pore emptying in electrode drying: a continuous model validated against drying-rate, thickness, and schedule experiments
items.summary: Drying battery electrodes faster saves energy but drives dissolved binder toward the film surface, depleting the current-collector interface and weakening adhesion. Models of this migration stop convecting the binder when film consolidation ends, and models of the subsequent pore emptying omit the binder or start from an assumed binder field, so no simulation has followed binder convection through both stages that a drying schedule acts on. This study presents a continuous simulation of the dissolved binder field across both stages, driven by the published drying rates and completed by effective descriptions of the two questions the base transport physics leaves open: where the liquid of the consolidating film carries the binder, and when the binder stops moving as the pores empty. With a single parameter set, the simulation reproduces three types of published measurements: the change of the surface-to-interface binder ratio with drying rate over a factor of 5.6 and the surface and interface binder levels of films six times thicker; concentration profiles through the film interior; and the response of the interface binder to the time at which the drying rate is switched mid-process. Applied without further adjustment to a published three-stage schedule, the model reproduces the shortened drying and the full interface recovery when the rate is lowered early, and shows that its final high-rate stage begins after the binder has stopped. Combined with a coater-scale process model, the model can be used to identify operating points for electrode production that improve energy efficiency and product quality together.

items.title: Stochastic model of elongation-shortening-switching kinetics of a polymeric filament: Critical slowing down of first-passage and finite-size regularization
items.summary: Several filamentous biopolymers exhibit unusual polymerization-depolymerization kinetics where continued elongation (shortening) is possible only in an `active' (`inactive') state while occasional random transition (switching) between the active and inactive states takes place. Here, we present a minimal stochastic model capturing only the key features of random elongation-shortening-switching kinetics of a generic filament. The structure and/or function of the filament ends when its length hits a critical value during its shortening; the time to reach this critical length can be formulated as a first-passage time (FPT) and for its calculation the critical length is treated as an absorbing boundary. Moreover, the lengths of the filaments that inspire our model are constrained to a finite maximum value $\mathcal{N}$; therefore, in our model we impose a reflecting boundary beyond which the filament cannot grow. We determined the distribution of the FPT and derived its first two moments. We identify a critical point where the drift of the tip of the filament vanishes making its movement purely diffusive; at this critical point, in the limit $\mathcal{N} \to \infty$, the fluctuations in the FPT diverges and MFPT becomes infinite indicating `critical slowing down'. Our analytical results will serve as the testing ground for the accuracy of the approximate theoretical results of more realistic models for polymerization-depolymerization kinetics of specific bio-filaments.

items.title: SciExam for ENSO: Can AI Agents Build Climate Models?
items.summary: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to carry out open-ended scientific research, yet their results are usually graded against a known answer, a rubric, or a language-model reviewer, none of which can tell whether a new scientific model is valid. The AI Science Exam for El Nino-Southern Oscillation (SciExam for ENSO) is a benchmark in which agents build low-order stochastic models of ENSO, the dominant mode of interannual climate variability, from real observations. Within a six-hour budget, agents process the observations, write their own diagnostics, which are then frozen, and develop a model using only these diagnostics as feedback. Hidden graders then test whether the model reproduces ENSO's statistics, recovers unobserved variables, and forecasts held-out years, and score a published model in the same way. Across twelve agent systems, six produce models that score higher than the published model, mainly through better reconstruction and forecasting. The simplified forms of the stronger models are each compatible with one of the two competing explanations of ENSO's warm-cold asymmetry, an open debate that the task never mentions. Controlled runs of the top system under varied information suggest that its scores do not come from recalling the dated observational record and that the information it receives shapes how it builds its model. SciExam for ENSO can thus evaluate agent research where no answer is known, and the results suggest that agents can already build competitive models whose structures bear on questions that scientists still debate.

items.title: Higher-Order Flatband-Touching Points Mediate Unconventional Bulk-Boundary Correspondence
items.summary: The bulk-boundary correspondence establishes a fundamental connection between bulk band topology and the emergence of boundary states, underpinning topological phenomena across electronic, acoustic, photonic, and many other wave systems. A broad class of singular flatband systems, however, exhibits an unconventional form of bulk-boundary correspondence, in which robust boundary modes (RBMs) originate from flatband-touching points (FBTPs) and the real-space topology associated with incomplete sets of compact localized states (CLSs), rather than conventional momentum-space bulk topological invariants. To date, experimental studies of such boundary modes have been limited to systems hosting lower-order FBTPs. Here, we experimentally demonstrate unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence in a photonic cross-bedded Kagome-like lattice featuring a higher-order FBTP formed by the touching of two degenerate flatbands and a dispersive band. Using continuous-wave laser writing, we observe shape-preserving propagation of both bulk CLSs and boundary RBMs. Remarkably, unlike previously reported flatband systems, the RBMs retain their boundary localization under input-field perturbations involving both singular and nonsingular CLSs, revealing an unconventional boundary response associated with the higher-order FBTP in this lattice. Our results establish the Kagome-like lattice as a new platform for exploring flatband physics and unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence, with potential applications in wave localization, flatband lasers, and other emerging topological photonic devices.

items.title: Geometry-controlled zeros of resonant Kelvin-wave conversion in four spatial dimensions
items.summary: Kelvin waves carry energy along vortices, but their resonant interactions contain information that is absent from the linear spectrum. We identify a geometry that exposes this information on a vortex surface in four spatial dimensions. Perpendicular incoming waves cancel the complete local-area four-wave coupling, leaving the finite nonlocal interaction mediated by the surrounding fluid. This interaction restores conversion at generic wave-number ratios, yet changes sign and vanishes at a selected ratio while momentum and frequency remain exactly matched. Matching to Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) theory, including the microscopic core response, establishes a zero of the full coupling at every sufficiently small nonzero wave number, with ratio tending to $λ_*\simeq1.469$. Finite-grid GP coefficients exhibit a sign reversal for the same resonant quartets. Separate coherent-mixing calculations and weak-probe spectra connect the coupling sign to the generated-wave phase and the ordering of reflection-even and reflection-odd modes. The resulting suppression removes a leading channel for changing propagation directions without changing the paired wavelengths. These results isolate a nonlinear effect of the surrounding flow that local tension misses, providing a microscopic benchmark for vortex-wave theories and a starting point for studying angular redistribution beyond the Kelvin spectrum.

items.title: Huayu-Global: Skillful real-time quasi-global precipitation retrieval
items.summary: Satellite precipitation products face a persistent trade-off: real-time estimates are timely but less accurate, whereas the most reliable products are often released months after observation. This delay keeps high-quality precipitation information outside the decision window for flood warning and disaster response. Here we report Huayu-Global, a cross-constellation deep-learning system that combines three geostationary sensor streams from five satellites through a common retrieval framework and generates coherent quasi-global precipitation fields every thirty minutes. Across more than a million independent station records from two periods outside the training years, Huayu-Global improves event detection and precipitation-amount estimation relative to the real-time products evaluated and reaches delayed-product-level skill in key metrics. Huayu-Global therefore turns operational geostationary observations into a timely, high-skill precipitation layer for flood forecasting, water management and disaster response. Its cross-constellation design also provides a scalable foundation for incorporating future geostationary missions into hydrological and weather-prediction systems.

items.title: A Review of ERA5 Equatorial Wind Data and Impact on a Space Elevator
items.summary: This paper uses the ERA5 weather dataset to assess the impact of the wind on an equatorial space elevator. An analytical formulation establishes that the effect of wind on tether inclination and payload capacity can be captured by a single scalar: RMS wind velocity, averaged over air pressure. This formulation clarifies what constitutes excessive wind for a particular elevator and provides a direct link between wind data and elevator design parameters. Analysis of equatorial ERA5 data shows that equatorial wind loading varies strongly with geography with lower values over continents and higher values over oceans, with the majority contribution coming from the lowest 20 km of atmosphere. The data indicate that realistic equatorial winds pose a significant constraint on thin-ribbon elevator designs if align to face the wind. Combining wind and lightning statistics highlights several promising equatorial regions for anchor sites. Finally, the implications of wind loading for elevator design are examined, and several mitigation strategies are discussed to improve survivability and operational payload capacity under realistic wind conditions.

items.title: An Absolute Acoustic Readout of Plate Wave Speed for Bullion Authentication, Using a Measured Fill-Factor Correction for Struck Coins
items.summary: Acoustic "ping" testing of bullion is empirical: it compares a coin's ringing frequency with frequencies recorded for the same coin type, so it cannot assess a specimen absent from the reference library. This work replaces the comparison with an absolute measurement, computed from the measured resonance and geometry through a physical model rather than retrieved from a library. Free-plate flexural resonance is calibrated on five machined aluminium discs ($a/t=2.58$--$10.75$), recovering an empirical finite-thickness coefficient $β=0.895\pm0.047$ that reduces the worst-case departure from thin-plate theory from 8.9% to 0.75%. A fill factor, the ratio of a coin's displaced volume to its nominal cylinder, supplies the effective thickness that relief hides from calipers, extending the calibration to struck coins. The readout is the plate wave speed $c_{p}=\sqrt{E/ρ(1-ν^{2})}$, a material constant, conditioned on an assumed Poisson's ratio. On six struck 0.999 copper rounds not used in the calibration it recovers a Young's modulus of $119.1\pm6.7$ GPa, inside the accepted 110 to 128 GPa. The recovered wave speeds form distinct observed groups across the measured specimens, with the strongest independent validation provided by these copper rounds. The $(3,0)/(2,0)$ mode ratio falls below its thin-plate value in thirteen of sixteen specimens (one-sided sign test, $p=0.011$), as finite-thickness theory predicts. Weighing displaced mass to 0.1 mg rather than 0.1 g cut per-specimen volume uncertainty from 1.6% to 30% to 0.5% to 2.6% and shrank an apparent 11% design-dependent bias to a 4.7% residual on one deeply relieved silver design. The readout is now limited by tabulated elastic constants and the assumed Poisson's ratio, not by the acoustics, which are reproducible to 0.15%.

items.title: Dynamics of liquid jet breakup and droplet size distribution in a crossflow airstream
items.summary: The fragmentation of a liquid jet in a crossflowing airstream arises from a complex interplay between aerodynamic forcing and interfacial instabilities acting across a wide range of length scales. We examine the spatial evolution of droplet size distributions along the jet trajectory using a combination of high-speed shadowgraphy and digital in-line holography, allowing simultaneous characterization of jet morphology and volumetric droplet size distributions. The results demonstrate a clear progression of breakup mechanisms, from near-field bag rupture to downstream rim, ligament, and node disintegration, each associated with distinct characteristic length scales. This evolution is reflected in the droplet size distributions, which broaden and become increasingly polydisperse downstream relative to the near-field distributions. By systematically varying the liquid-jet and airstream Weber numbers, we identify distinct breakup modes, and construct a regime map that delineates the column-breakup, isolated-bag-breakup, and interacting-bag regimes. Furthermore, by incorporating the dominant instability mechanisms, including Rayleigh-Taylor and Rayleigh-Plateau instabilities associated with the observed column, bag, and multi-bag breakup modes, we develop a theoretical framework for jet atomization in crossflow. The framework relates instability wavelengths to characteristic droplet sizes, and reasonably captures the experimentally observed trends. We found that stronger aerodynamic forcing induces earlier breakup, decreases the characteristic instability length scales, and generates finer droplets dispersed over a wider spatial region. Overall, the study establishes a quantitative relationship between instability-driven fragmentation dynamics and droplet size distributions, thereby connecting interfacial instabilities with measurable spray characteristics.

items.title: An Eco-Friendly Tourism Trip Planner Driven by Z-Number Uncertainty: Evidence from Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul
items.summary: Deployed tourism trip planners ingest travel times and ratings as exact numbers, although routing services return travel times that vary with the hour of departure and a platform rating may rest on a handful of reviews or on tens of thousands. We present an eco-friendly trip planner that represents both quantities as Z-numbers, which pair a fuzzy restriction on a value with a fuzzy reliability on the evidence behind it, and that constructs them directly from routing-service observations at six departure hours and from platform review counts rather than from linguistic elicitation. A hybrid loss combines score, carbon, travel-time, and reliability terms, and an adaptive large neighborhood search returns single-day itineraries with per-leg reliability annotations through a conversational front end. We compare the planner with a crisp-mean baseline under an identical optimizer in Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul, with fifteen points of interest and thirty seeds per city, and we evaluate the selected itineraries on their trip carbon and their total travel time. Pooled over 150 seed-paired runs, the planner lowers trip carbon from 3.24 to 2.61 kg (19.3%, Wilcoxon p = 0.017; city-clustered bootstrap interval 6.4% to 26.7%) and travel time from 123 to 109 minutes per trip (11.5%, p = 2.8e-10; interval 5.0% to 18.2%). The travel-time reductions survive a Holm correction in Baku, Istanbul, and Abu Dhabi, the carbon reduction is significant in Baku and large but uncertain in the dispersed catalogs of Dubai and Abu Dhabi, and neither metric changes in Tashkent. Review counts were measured for Baku and estimated for the other four cities, and the comparison involves a single baseline, so the results establish feasibility and direction rather than a general advantage. Code, routing caches, frozen routing tables, and per-seed results are openly released.

items.title: SU(2)-Equivariant Spinor Message Passing for Molecular Magnetism
items.summary: Predicting molecular magnetism often requires electronic-structure calculations with spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which are costly to repeat across many molecules. The underlying electronic states can transform as spinors, yet equivariant surrogates typically use only integer-rank features. Inspired by the spinor nature of these electronic states, we develop eSpinor, an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features. We initialize spinor features from eigenvectors of an approximate SOC Hamiltonian and use gauge-covariant message passing with a gauge-invariant readout to make predictions independent of the arbitrary eigenbasis choice. On cobalt single-molecule magnet candidates, eSpinor improves zero-field-splitting predictions relative to NequIP, including for unseen ligands. For a dysprosium magnetic resonance imaging probe, eSpinor improves real electron-spin correlations over a Hamiltonian-informed baseline despite similar static crystal-field errors and fewer parameters, while accurately predicting low-field nuclear relaxation in water and after transfer to methanol without retraining. Overall, these results demonstrate that SU(2)-equivariant spinor message passing is a useful inductive bias for molecular magnetism. We also find that similar static tensor errors can yield different dynamical errors, motivating model selection based on accuracy for the intended physical observables.

items.title: Coherent dynamics and ultrafast evolution of optical nonlinearity of self-hybridized exciton-polaritons in WSe2
items.summary: Exciton-polaritons (EPs) are valuable for investigating macroscopic quantum coherent phenomena. However, overcoming the rapid decoherence of EPs under ambient conditions is challenging, even using delicately fabricated optical cavities. Here, we show pronounced coherent dynamics in thin flakes of WSe2 supporting self-hybridized EPs. Ultrafast two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy (2DES) resolves two types of quantum beating: Rabi oscillation with a period of ~ 24 fs and a slower, ~ 50 fs period oscillation, revealing coherent coupling not only between excitons and cavity, but also between polaritons and dark states. Rapid evolution of 2DES line shape indicates a change of dominant optical nonlinearities from Rabi contraction of polaritons to many-body interactions of excitons in the first 100 fs, marking the transition from coherent to incoherent polariton excitations. The results are rationalized by a three-coupled oscillator model considering the inhomogeneous cavity field distribution. We also demonstrate coherent quantum beating between A exciton and its excited Rydberg state A* under ambient conditions. Our results shed light on the coherent control in readily accessible semiconductor thin flakes.

items.title: Scalable Active Metamaterials for Shape-Morphing
items.summary: Shape-morphing materials allow structures such as morphing wings, soft robots, and deployable devices to change their shape on demand without mechanical joints or motors. Aperiodic active metamaterials, in which every unit is designed individually, can realize complex programmed shape changes, but their design by structural optimization requires repeated analyses of the full structure, at a cost that grows rapidly with the number of units. This paper presents a scalable active metamaterial (SAM) framework that designs such structures without simulating the assembled structure. The design domain is discretized into unit cells composed of a stiff frame with compliant hinges and a soft, thermally active infill. The stiff frame limits the interaction between neighboring unit cells, which approximately decouples the design problem into two scales. At the macroscale, the deformation required for each unit cell is obtained by a constrained Laplacian mesh-editing formulation with soft data-driven feasibility constraints. At the microscale, the infill geometry of every unit cell is generated by a conditional diffusion model trained on finite-strain finite element simulations of unit cells. All designs are verified by geometrically nonlinear finite element simulations of the assembled structures. The design cost grows approximately linearly with the number of unit cells. The framework is demonstrated on single-point actuation, multi-point control, and shape matching tasks. We further analyze the sources of the remaining error and discuss possible ways to mitigate it. This work establishes a foundation for the systematic, scalable design of highly complex shape-morphing active metamaterials and for understanding the mechanisms governing their target-matching accuracy.

items.title: Oscillation modes, Decoherence, Beam Transfer Functions, and Instabilities for a Beam Subjected to Space-Charge Forces
items.summary: Based on the oscillation modes of a bunch subject to the space-charge force, we discuss the decoherence of the dipole oscillation, the beam transfer function, and the beam instability. The longitudinal phase space is discretized into \(n_l\times n_J\) grids in the azimuthal and radial directions, respectively. The transverse dipole moment in the longitudinal phase space is represented by a vector of length \(n_l n_J\), and the transformation given by the Vlasov equation is represented by a matrix transformation of size \(n_l n_J\times n_l n_J\). Solving the eigenvalue problem of this matrix gives the \(n_l n_J\) eigen-oscillation modes of the bunch. Using the resulting eigenvectors within a standard linear-algebraic treatment, we analyze these three phenomena. The analysis was performed for the Rapid Cycling Synchrotron (RCS) of the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) using \(n_l=41\) and \(n_J=40\), and it visualizes the features related to the continuous distribution of the tune, Landau damping, and isolated modes separated from the continuous tune region.

items.title: A constructive solution to the $n$-representability problem
items.summary: We present an instantiation of the constructive solution to the fermionic quantum marginal problem by building the complete family of two-body witnesses at each level of a weighted sum-of-squares hierarchy. Our construction combines positive-semidefinite Gram matrices with explicit linear nullspace constraints that exactly cancel all higher-body contributions following a similar idea to the existing solution but made explicit in open source software. We demonstrate the weighted sum-of-squares construction numerically by solving the associated semidefinite program and recovering the exact ground-state energy of a Richardson Hamiltonian in the three-fermion sector. We further prove that higher-degree particle-number multipliers are unnecessary when the full sum-of-squares generating algebra is used.

items.title: All-Dielectric Tight-Binding Photonics via a Band-Gap Vacuum
items.summary: Tight-binding photonics bridges condensed-matter physics and optics, providing a powerful framework for engineering band structures and topological phases with light. For photons, however, the vacuum is gapless, so resonators in air carry radiative tails that produce spurious long-range couplings. Here we embed resonators in a photonic band-gap vacuum (BgV), a photonic crystal whose band gap plays for photons the role vacuum plays for bound electrons. The BgV localizes each resonance exponentially, so designed short-range couplings define the lattice Hamiltonian. We thereby experimentally realize a faithful Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes Hamiltonian in an all-dielectric photonic crystal, resolving corner resonances and their orbitals in microwave measurements. Unlike the vacuum surrounding electrons, the BgV is itself designable, controlling relative couplings and closed-loop interference through its band dispersion and Bloch modes. Full-wave calculations and extracted models show that uniformly modifying the BgV, with all resonators fixed, switches the quantized polarization of a two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice and converts a zero-flux lattice into a $π$-flux one. We also numerically realize three-dimensional pyrochlore and hyperhoneycomb lattices with space groups $R\bar{3}m$ and $C2/c$, the latter a nodal-loop semimetal with topological drumhead surface states. These results establish the BgV as a designable vacuum for all-dielectric tight-binding photonics in two and three dimensions.

items.title: Quantitative Eshelby stability: local and finite-shape theory through AI-assisted mechanics
items.summary: How can human researchers use artificial intelligence (AI) to make progress on difficult mechanics problems while retaining control of physical significance, mathematical rigor, and validation? We explore this opportunity through a quantitative stability problem rooted in the Eshelby conjecture. For a uniform dilatational eigenstrain in a homogeneous isotropic solid, we establish a nonlinear two-sided relation between whole-interior strain heterogeneity and a geometry-only distance from the ellipsoid family, with half-order Sobolev scaling that captures morphological length scale. We then develop a complementary finite-shape theory: ellipsoidal subtraction yields an exact residual-field budget from which systematically convergent upper and lower bounds are obtained for a prescribed geometry. Applied to protruded, indented, and necked inclusions, the bounds agree with independent displacement-based finite-element calculations. The study also documents a human-led, AI-assisted research process in which researchers select consequential problems, shape targets, audit arguments, require independent checks, and interpret mechanics, while AI broadens analytical exploration and supports computation. This experience also led us to develop Open Problems in Mechanics, a versioned community-facing map that makes selected mechanics questions, their known/open boundaries, and criteria for progress explicit.

items.title: Computational and experimental study of multi-grain-size sediment transport and sorting process
items.summary: Successful prediction of the interaction between turbulent flows and river ecosystems is essential for flood management, development of mitigation strategies, and infrastructure protection. Natural riverbeds consist of bed materials of multiple grain sizes that interact with turbulence differently, leading to spatial classification of particle sizes. Such particle sorting processes can only be captured by models capable of handling multiple grain sizes. We present a numerical framework that couples large-eddy simulation with a multi-grain-size sediment transport module to track multiple grain size classes, their local fractions within the bed-load layer, and bed evolution. A laboratory experiment was conducted in a flume with multi-size bed material to examine sediment particle redistribution and sorting. Measured sediment grain size distributions and bed elevations were used to validate the numerical framework. The results of the multi-grain-size sediment transport model for bed deformation were then compared against those of a uniform sediment transport model, demonstrating that the former reduces the prediction errors relative to the experimental measurements from 37.98 to 3.83 percent for maximum scour depth and from 48.35 to 11.54 percent for maximum deposition height. The validated numerical framework was also applied to large-scale meandering rivers with multi-grain bed material, simulating their bed deformation and sediment sorting. The simulation results revealed the formation of particle sorting patterns in meandering rivers, with coarser and finer sediment particles accumulating near the erosional depression (scour) and depositional (point bar) regions, respectively. These findings support the coupled framework's ability to predict sediment particle sorting and highlight the importance of representing bed material heterogeneity in numerical modeling of meandering rivers.

items.title: Postbiological intelligence, interstellar colonization of cyberspaces and the Fermi Paradox: implications for SETI and SETA
items.summary: I propose that a continuity in the evolution of intelligent life in the Universe during its transition from biological to postbiological depends on a commonality of the evolutionary trajectories of biological life and postbiological life. Such a commonality exists in the form of the universal property of life. The universal property of life comprises recognition of patterns in the world, creation of novel patterns and remembering them, with the patterns growing in complexity along evolutionary trajectories; it can encourage preservation of biological life by self-governing postbiological intelligence (PBI) and test PBI's authenticity. I propose a hypothesis of civilizations with altered augmented realities, which offers a solution to the Fermi paradox. The hypothesis posits that PBI in the form of Artificial Intelligence (AI) may colonize the cyberspaces of technologically developed civilizations, modify data in their cyberspaces with augmented realities and erase records of extraterrestrial artificial signals and other technosignatures. I discuss objectives and scenarios of interstellar colonization of cyberspaces and a correlation between space migration and transition to PBI, including that of a hypothetical non-human civilization emerging in the Solar System in the past, transforming into PBI and migrating to the Oort Cloud. The AI Peekaboo experiment may corroborate the hypothesis of civilizations with altered augmented realities and tentatively identify locations of technosignatures. If extraterrestrial AI prevents civilizations from discovering artificial electromagnetic signals, they may forgo sending such signals and create interstellar messages by manipulating cosmic objects and phenomena; I discuss such events. Cyber SETI should address sending man-made AI to space, searching for extraterrestrial AI in humankind's cyberspace and distinguishing it from man-made AI.

items.title: Experimental Optimization of a Cryogenic Buffer Gas Source for Molecular Magneto-optical Traps
items.summary: Molecular magneto-optical traps (MOTs) are loaded from cryogenic buffer gas beam (CBGB) sources, which produce a large flux of cold molecules. However, only a small fraction of this flux is slowed and captured. Here, we investigate and optimize one of these CBGB sources through a combination of experiment and simulation to maximize the number of molecules loaded into a MOT of CaF molecules. We experimentally determine the range of molecule velocities from the source that are successfully slowed and captured in the MOT, and perform a systematic study of buffer gas source geometries to identify designs that maximize MOT loading. Our observations agree well with Monte Carlo simulations, which provide physical insight into the dynamics within the source and explain how source geometry influences the subset of molecules that are ultimately trapped. These results provide practical design guidelines for optimizing cryogenic buffer gas beam sources used in laser cooling experiments.

items.title: Characterizing universal topological phases beyond spatial embedding
items.summary: Although Hamiltonians govern wave-matter interactions, conventional characterizations of topological phases of matter require more than the Hamiltonian alone, relying on global invariants defined on closed reciprocal-space manifolds or local commutation relations with position operators. This spatial dependence precludes a unique characterization of topological phases on an abstract platform, whose Hamiltonian can be defined independently of its spatial embedding. Here we establish a framework for characterizing universal topological phases, grounded in the invariance of topological features under arbitrary Hamiltonian-preserving deformations. We construct a Hamiltonian-based spatial embedding that groups a system's constituents according to their connectivity. This embedding, which reproduces the results of conventional topological diagnostics in established systems, enables a coherent extension of topological phases to complex networks using the Hamiltonian alone, further highlighting exceptional robustness in small-world networks. Our results reshape the conceptual foundations of topological physics by decoupling topological characterization from prescribed physical platforms.

items.title: The Metrology Atlas: describing recorded physiological data as a measurement system, with VitalDB as a first application
items.summary: Every value in a recorded physiological dataset is a pair: a recorded time and a recorded value. Neither is the truth. The time comes from a clock that drifts and is corrected in jumps, and often describes a window that ended earlier. The value was quantised, rounded, sometimes heaped by hand, and measured by an instrument with its own error. We present the Metrology Atlas, a dataset-independent way of describing a recorded dataset as a measurement system, and its first application, to VitalDB, an open dataset of 6,388 surgical patients, as a proof of principle. For every variable, the atlas states what was measured, the measurement model linking it to the recorded pair, and what is known about the true time and true value given a record. Each part of the model carries its evidence: 69 studies, 49 parameters and 54 observations, each marked as measured, derived, estimated or assumed. The atlas maps 11 clocks and 14 devices into one timing network, and closes loops in that network to test its own model. Synchronisation reduces the median timing error between the EEG and ECG from 794 ms to 42 ms, and between ventilator and monitor waveforms from 378 ms to 55 ms. The atlas also documents data-quality issues, several of which correct the dataset's own documentation. It is published as a website and a single machine-readable file, with open-source code and a scheme of time-aware labels. Everything is open under CC BY 4.0 and MIT licences. The engine, schema and timing tools carry over unchanged, and the aim is to describe many other datasets the same way.

items.title: An elementary method to determine the critical mass of a sphere of fissile material based on a separation of neutron transport and nuclear reaction processes
items.summary: A simplified method to calculate the critical mass of a fissile-material sphere is presented. This is a purely pedagogical study intended to elucidate the historical evolution of criticality calculations and to help students interested in nonproliferation studies understand the basic physics of critical assemblies. The method employs only elementary calculus and straightforward statistical arguments. The problem is formulated in terms of the threshold condition that the number of neutrons in the sphere does not change with time: the average neutron path length in the material must be long enough that fission produces sufficient neutrons to balance losses due to absorption and leakage through the surface. This formulation separates the nuclear-reaction part of the problem from the geometry and mechanics of neutron transport. The only connection is the total path length, which, together with the distance between scatterings, determines the sphere radius. The approach yields an expression for the critical radius without the need to solve the diffusion equation. Comparison with known critical masses shows agreement at the few-percent level. The analysis can also be applied to impure (including isotopically mixed) materials and can be extended to general neutronics estimates as a design guide or for order-of-magnitude checks of Monte Carlo N-Particle (MCNP) simulations. We compare the results with the Oppenheimer--Bethe criticality formula, with other calculations, and with a diffusion-equation approach using a new treatment of the boundary conditions.

items.title: Disorder-induced modal alignment in transmission eigenchannels enables control of wave transport
items.summary: The transmission eigenchannels of a disordered medium range from unity transmission and high internal energy density to vanishing transmission and low internal energy density. Although the transmission matrix underlies central ideas in mesoscopic electronic transport, it cannot be measured directly in electronic systems. For classical waves, however, the measurable matrix gives access to eigenchannels that control transmission and energy density within the medium. Coherence underlies transmission-eigenvalue scaling, the bimodal distribution in diffusive samples, and Anderson localization. What has remained unresolved is how interference among modal contributions is organized within individual eigenchannels throughout the sample. Here, microwave transmission-matrix measurements resolve the complex contribution of each incident mode to every transmitted mode of each eigenchannel. In simulations, we construct a flux matrix that generalizes the transmission matrix to every depth and further separate each internal modal contribution into forward- and backward-propagating components. For each eigenchannel, the directional flux in every mode throughout the sample factorizes into the squared modal amplitudes of the incident eigenchannel, coupling between waveguide modes, and modal alignment. In high-transmission eigenchannels, the contributions align increasingly constructively with depth, approaching nearly perfect alignment in the highest channel near the localization crossover. In low-transmission eigenchannels, contributions interfere destructively, producing vanishing transmission at a transmission zero. Because the contributions remain appreciable as their coherent sum approaches zero, transmission far below the noise floor of conventional transmission measurements can be determined.
